title: Is Iren Stock a Buy Now? - The Globe and Mail
content: Iren is transitioning away from Bitcoin mining to AI cloud services. The company is expanding its workforce and saw AI cloud services revenue rise from $16.4 million in 2025 to $128.8 million in 2026. Iren secured a $9.7 billion cloud services deal with Microsoft, along with additional contracts with various AI companies. Demand for artificial intelligence (AI) is growing and creating massive opportunities for companies with the compute capacity to run training and inference workloads. Iren(NASDAQ: IREN) has traditionally used its compute capacity to mine Bitcoin, but the company has pivoted from cryptocurrency mining to providing cloud services to help technology companies manage workloads. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Iren is winding down its Bitcoin operations by the end of this year and leaning fully into managing AI workloads. With the stock trading down about 37% from its 52-week high, is now a good time to buy? Let's dive into the business and opportunity ahead to find out. For years, Iren focused on mining Bitcoin using ASIC (custom integrated circuit chips built for a specific task rather than general computing) hardware. However, the company is undergoing a massive strategic shift, redirecting its computing infrastructure toward AI cloud services. This shift has had a couple of impacts on Iren. For one, the company has recorded massive losses relating to this transition. For its fiscal year 2026 (ending June 30), Iren recorded a net loss of $702.6 million, a massive increase from its net profit of $86.9 million the year before. A major reason for this loss was a $638.8 million noncash asset impairment charge for decommissioning and writing down its mining hardware. On the flip side, Iren's AI cloud services revenue has surged. In 2026, the company's cloud revenue reached $128.8 million, up from $16.4 million the year before. As part of its pivot, the company's workforce nearly tripled during the year, and it has brought in C-suite leaders from technology giants like Nvidia, Amazon Web Services, Oracle, and Alphabet's Google. Iren's pivot is well underway. In November 2025, the company signed a $9.7 billion cloud services deal with Microsoft. As part of the deal, Iren will provide large-scale GPU clusters to handle 200 megawatts (MW) of critical IT load at its Childress, Texas, campus. Iren expects the five-year deal to deliver roughly $1.94 billion in annualized run rate revenue when fully commissioned. In addition, Iren has contracts with other AI companies, including Perplexity, Cohere, Together AI, Fal AI, Higgsfield AI, and Prometheus. Iren has made an important pivot toward AI cloud services, which should drive more growth than its previous Bitcoin mining operations. As part of this pivot, the company is incurring massive costs, including projected capital expenditures of $25 billion to $30 billion in 2027 as it upgrades and expands its data center hubs to support powerful Nvidia chips. The company is using debt and customer pre-payments, which fund about half of its GPU capital expenditures up front on recent deals. For conservative investors seeking capital preservation or dividends, Iren is a stock to avoid. However, for growth-focused investors looking to play the booming demand for compute from AI hyperscalers, Iren is a solid stock to capitalize on this trend. title: Can Microsoft Stock Keep Earning Like This? - Trefis
content: Microsoft (MSFT) is coming off the most profitable stretch it has posted in years, and its stock trades at $493.95, about 92% of its 52-week high. Nothing here is broken. The risk is quieter than that. The spending that came with those margins is still climbing, and the company has already told shareholders what it expects that to do to fiscal 2027. Net margin over the trailing twelve months is 40.3%, the highest in at least five years and well above a 36.8% three-year average. Operating margin runs 46.8% against a 45.3% three-year average, near the top of its multi-year range. Revenue of $331.8 billion grew 17.8% year over year, so none of this came from a shrinking business. Margins at a peak rarely stay there. This peak arrives with a specific and growing bill, and that bill is the Azure build-out. Azure revenue grew 43% in fiscal Q4 2026, and management says customer demand still exceeds available capacity. Company-wide, the build-out took $41 billion of capital expenditure in that one quarter (including equipment acquired under leases), roughly two-thirds of it on what management calls short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs. Against $55.4 billion in cash from operations, cash actually paid for property and equipment was $35.8 billion, yielding $19.6 billion in free cash flow. The bill is already visible in the margin. The company’s gross margin was 67% in fiscal Q4 2026, down year over year, and management attributes the decline to the sales mix shift toward Azure and the AI infrastructure spending behind it, offset only partly by efficiency gains. Capital expenditure is guided higher again in fiscal 2027. Management guides fiscal 2027 operating margins down less than one point, while still expecting double-digit revenue and operating income growth. Operating income can keep rising while the margin falls. It is the margin the price is leaning on. On price-to-sales the stock trades at 11.1, about 71% of the way up its own 10-year range. That guide already carries a change extending the assumed useful life of data centers and office buildings from 15 to 25 years. While management expects only a minimal cushion to fiscal 2027 operating income, the greater impact shifts data-center leases out of reported capital expenditure—meaning headline capex growth appears somewhat softer than the actual build-out pace. The primary downside risk is valuation compression rather than an operational breakdown. The stock returned 20.2% over the past three months to get back near its high, but only 0.6% over the past twelve months, against 19.3% for the S&P 500 over that same window. That twelve-month gap against the index is the cost so far. The stock’s worst peak-to-trough fall inside that year was 34.5%, suggesting that even modest multiple contraction could occur without an operational miss. The line to watch is the Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage, which ran 65% in fiscal Q4 2026 and was down year over year, and which management guides to be roughly stable quarter over quarter. If it keeps sliding while capital expenditure grows, the margin peak is already past. Implied volatility sits near the 44th percentile of its 52-week range, indicating that the options market has not yet priced in elevated downside risk. Now, our Option Implied Volatility screen shows what is priced. Probably not on any particular morning. Microsoft ended June with more than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats and generated $59.3 billion in quarterly cloud revenue. title: Microsoft Sits Flat at $493.51 as Meta Rips 5.75% and Alphabet Sheds 3.04% - TradingNEWS
content: Microsoft (MSFT) trades at $493.51, down $0.44 or 0.09%, against Tuesday's close of $493.95. Forty-four cents of movement on a $3.67 trillion company, on a day when Meta ripped 5.75% to $648.77 and Alphabet shed 3.04% to $328.07. That non-reaction is the most informative thing about the stock today. Meta launched Muse, a paid consumer AI agent, Tuesday evening. The market took roughly $135 billion out of Alphabet and put roughly $107 billion into Meta. Microsoft moved less than half a percent. The market has decided that whatever Muse is, it does not touch Microsoft's business — and it is right, because Microsoft sells AI to IT departments on seat licenses and consumption contracts, not to consumers through app stores. Underneath that indifference sits a stock that has already had its repricing. Microsoft closed at $390.54 the day before its fiscal fourth-quarter report on July 29 and jumped 8.13% to $422.30 in after-hours trading, then extended to roughly 17% the following session. It has since worked to $493.51 — a 26.4% advance in six weeks — and sits 10.9% below its 52-week high of $553.72 against a low of $349.20. The report that produced it delivered numbers that ended a specific argument. Azure grew 43% and crossed $100 billion in annual revenue. Commercial remaining performance obligation reached $678 billion, up 84%. Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats. Annual revenue exceeded $331 billion, up 18%. The report also delivered the number that will define the next four quarters: fiscal 2027 capital expenditure guidance of $255 billion to $260 billion, against $190 billion committed for 2026 — a 35% increase in a spending program that was already the largest in corporate history. The thesis running through this piece: Microsoft is the only hyperscaler that has shown the market a demand backlog large enough to justify its capital program, and the $678 billion RPO figure is why the stock trades at 27.5 times earnings while peers with worse cash conversion trade at similar or higher multiples. The question the October 27 report answers is whether the backlog converts fast enough to absorb $260 billion of spending. The recent price sequence shows a stock consolidating after a violent move rather than reversing it. Microsoft closed at $499.70 on Friday, September 4. Markets were closed Monday for Labor Day. Tuesday brought a $5.75 decline of 1.15% to $493.95, with the session ranging from $490.15 to $495.19 and the stock opening $6.00 below the prior close. Wednesday has produced 44 cents of movement to $493.51. That is a stock that gave back a point on Tuesday and has done nothing since. The $490 level held on the only real test of the week. The broader tape is worse than the stock. The S&P 500 trades at 7,651.41, down 0.29%. The Nasdaq 100 sits at 29,372, off 0.46%. The Dow has shed 312 points or 0.59%. Apple is down 0.92% to $313.31, Amazon off 1.88% to $252.13, Alphabet down 3.04%, Nvidia lower by 0.47% at $224.67, Oracle off 0.44% at $161.81. Microsoft's 0.09% decline is better than every megacap peer except Meta and Tesla. On a day with Brent at $101.071, the 10-year yielding 4.8120% and a 60% probability of a Federal Reserve hike on September 16, holding flat is a genuine relative result for a high-multiple growth stock. The pre-market print at $492.82 and the near-flat regular session together describe an absence of sellers rather than an arrival of buyers. Volume has not been the story this week. The context that makes the current level meaningful is what it took to get here. Microsoft entered its July 29 earnings report down roughly 19% year to date, having beaten expectations in each of the three prior quarters and been punished each time — shares fell 3.01%, then 9.80%, then 5.00% following those beats. Investors had stopped believing that capital expenditure would convert into revenue. The fourth-quarter report broke that pattern in a single session. The stock is now up on the year and trading above its 200-day exponential moving average for the first time since the May-June selloff. Consolidating 26% higher after six weeks is what a stock does when the repricing is complete and the next catalyst is a quarter away. The chart is constructive with one obvious hurdle directly overhead. The 52-week range runs $349.20 to $553.72. At $493.51 the stock sits 41.3% above the low and 10.9% below the high — well into the upper half of its annual range and above its 200-day simple moving average, which it reclaimed following the July earnings report. The immediate resistance is $499.70, Friday's close and the round $500 handle sitting immediately above it. Microsoft has been rejected there this week, with Tuesday's session opening $6.00 below that close and never recovering it. Reclaiming $500 restores the short-term uptrend. Above that, the path runs toward the mid-$530s and then to the $553.72 high, which is 12.2% above current price. That high was set before the year-to-date drawdown and represents the pre-capex-panic valuation. Beneath price, $490.15 is Tuesday's low and the first genuine support — 0.7% below spot. It held cleanly on the only test this week. Below that, the stock has an open gap zone back toward the mid-$460s from the post-earnings run, and then the $422.30 area where the July repricing began. That level is 14.4% below current price and represents the floor of the current structure. The 200-day EMA sits well beneath, having been reclaimed in late July. A stock trading above aligned 20-day and 50-day moving averages, with the 200-day recovered, is in an uptrend by every standard definition. Momentum has cooled without breaking. The stock has fallen 1.18% over the past week and roughly 1.52% over the past month — a pause after a 26% six-week advance rather than distribution. That is healthy consolidation, and it is what a base looks like before the next leg. The technical signal from moving averages and momentum indicators currently reads as a buy on the daily timeframe. The level that matters most for the next quarter is $553.72. Clearing a 52-week high on a $3.67 trillion company requires a catalyst, and the only one on the calendar is the October 27 earnings report. Between now and then, the range from $490 to $500 is where the stock lives. The fiscal fourth quarter ended June 30 and the numbers were a clean beat on every headline metric. Revenue came in at $90.01 billion, up 18% year over year against consensus estimates of roughly $87.67 billion. Non-GAAP earnings per share printed $4.74 against a $4.24 consensus — a 11.8% beat. GAAP earnings per share reached $4.81 with net income of $35.77 billion, up from $27.23 billion and $3.65 per share in the year-ago quarter. Net income grew 31.4% on 18% revenue growth, which is operating leverage working in the right direction. The Productivity and Business Processes segment, covering Office, Dynamics and LinkedIn, produced $37.85 billion in revenue, up 14.3% and ahead of the $37.19 billion consensus. For the full fiscal year, annual revenue surpassed $331 billion, up 18%. Microsoft Cloud revenue exceeded $214 billion, up 27%. Azure crossed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time, growing 41% over the year. Set that against the third quarter for the trajectory. Q3 fiscal 2026 delivered revenue of $82.9 billion up 18%, operating income of $38.4 billion up 20%, and EPS of $4.27 against a $4.13 consensus. Azure grew 40% in that quarter, its fastest pace in over a year, with AI services accounting for roughly 16 percentage points of that growth. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $54.5 billion, up 29%. The AI annual revenue run rate stood at $37 billion, up 123%. Sequential acceleration from 40% to 43% Azure growth is the detail that mattered most, because it directly contradicted the decelerating-cloud narrative that had taken the stock down 19% year to date. Guidance extended the story. The chief financial officer projected 45% Azure growth at constant currency for fiscal first quarter, above the 41.4% consensus, and management provided fiscal 2027 guidance for double-digit revenue and operating income growth. The market response was the largest single-session repricing in the stock's recent history. Shares moved from $390.54 to $422.30 in after-hours trading, an 8.13% gain, and extended to roughly 17% the following day. That reaction followed three consecutive quarters where beats produced declines of 3.01%, 9.80% and 5.00%. Sentiment does not shift on one print unless the print answers the specific question the market was asking. This one did. Azure and other cloud services grew 43% year over year in the fourth quarter, ahead of the company's own guided range of 39% to 40%, and pushed the business past $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time. Both halves of that sentence carry weight. A 43% growth rate on a business at $100 billion of annual scale is extraordinary — the law of large numbers says growth should decelerate as the base expands, and Azure accelerated from 40% in the third quarter to 43% in the fourth. The composition is what makes it credible. In the third quarter, AI services accounted for roughly 16 percentage points of Azure's 40% growth. That means the non-AI base business was growing at roughly 24%, and the AI layer was additive rather than cannibalizing. The company's AI annual revenue run rate reached $37 billion in the third quarter, up 123%. Guidance for fiscal first quarter sits at 45% constant-currency Azure growth against a 41.4% consensus, with management expecting continued acceleration through the first half of fiscal 2027. A cloud business guiding to acceleration at $100 billion scale is a rare thing. The competitive comparison sharpens it. Amazon Web Services grew 37% to $42.23 billion in its second quarter, with the AI business at a $25 billion annualized run rate. Google Cloud grew 82% to $24.77 billion in Alphabet's second quarter. Azure is growing faster than AWS from a larger base and is roughly four times the size of Google Cloud. Google Cloud's 82% growth rate is faster, but it is compounding on a $24.77 billion quarterly base against Azure's $100 billion annual scale. The absolute dollar addition favors Microsoft substantially. What Azure growth actually determines is the capital conversion rate. The company is spending $190 billion in calendar 2026 and guiding to $255 billion to $260 billion in fiscal 2027 specifically to build Azure capacity. Azure growth is the only measure of how much of that spending is generating revenue in the same fiscal year. At 43% growth with 45% guided, the conversion is working. At 35% or below, the capex-to-revenue relationship breaks and the entire investment case comes under review. Commercial remaining performance obligation surged 84% year over year to $678 billion. That figure is the single most important disclosure in the fourth-quarter report and it is the reason Microsoft's stock behaved differently from Meta's and Alphabet's this earnings season. RPO measures contracted future revenue — money customers have committed to spend that has not yet been recognized. It is not a pipeline, not a forecast, and not a management estimate. It is signed business. At $678 billion against annual revenue of $331 billion, Microsoft is carrying slightly more than two years of total company revenue in contracted commitments. Growing that number 84% in twelve months means the commitments are being signed far faster than they are being consumed. This is what separates Microsoft from every other company in the AI capital cycle. Meta is spending $130 billion to $145 billion in 2026 with free cash flow at $784 million and no contracted backlog at all — its revenue is advertising, sold in real time. Alphabet spent $44.92 billion in a single quarter with free cash flow at negative $5.9 billion and suspended its buyback. Both are building capacity against expected demand. Microsoft is building capacity against $678 billion of signed demand. That distinction is why the market rewarded a similar capex number in Microsoft's case and punished it elsewhere. Infrastructure spending backed by concrete contractual commitments is investment. Infrastructure spending backed by conviction is a bet. The caveat is duration and cancellability. RPO includes multi-year contracts stretching over horizons that give customers room to renegotiate, and a portion of it relates to arrangements with AI customers whose own funding depends on capital markets remaining open. An 84% increase concentrated in a small number of very large agreements carries counterparty risk that a broad enterprise base does not. Microsoft has not disclosed the concentration. That is the disclosure worth pressing for on October 27. For now, $678 billion is a genuine moat and it is what the current 27.5 times multiple is paying for. Microsoft 365 Copilot surpassed 30 million paid seats, up from more than 20 million as of April, with net seat additions more than doubling sequentially and user satisfaction scores doubling over the last three quarters. Ten million net paid seats added in a single quarter, with the pace of additions doubling, is the strongest consumer or enterprise AI adoption datapoint any company has disclosed. At the pricing levels these seats typically carry, 30 million paid seats implies an annual run rate in the neighborhood of $10 billion. GitHub Copilot now has 50 million users. Hundreds of enterprise customers have purchased millions of seats for high-end E7 productivity bundles. The more consequential development is structural rather than numerical. Microsoft is introducing usage-based billing models for Copilot, Cowork and GitHub Copilot alongside per-seat licensing. That changes the revenue model in a way that expands the addressable market meaningfully. Per-seat licensing caps revenue at the number of employees an organization has. Usage-based billing does not. An enterprise with 10,000 employees can only buy 10,000 seats, but it can consume an unbounded amount of agent compute if the agents are doing work that previously required more people. Converting from seats to consumption is how a software company escapes the ceiling of its customer's headcount. The architectural approach behind it is a mixed-model design that lets enterprises use frontier models for their strengths, low-cost models for efficiency, and train their own — the same pattern Microsoft uses internally in Copilot and GitHub Copilot, now being made available to customers. The comparison to Meta's Muse is instructive precisely because it is not competitive. Muse is a consumer subscription sold to individuals for personal tasks. Copilot is enterprise software sold to IT departments with security review, procurement cycles and multi-year commitments. Different buyer, different sales motion, different revenue durability. Enterprise revenue is stickier and slower. Consumer revenue is faster and churns. Microsoft holds the former, and that is why 30 million paid seats is a more durable number than any consumer agent adoption figure will be. The risk is that agent capability commoditizes and per-seat pricing collapses toward the cost of inference. The usage-based pivot is Microsoft's hedge against exactly that. Fiscal 2027 capital expenditure guidance sits at $255 billion to $260 billion, against $190 billion committed for calendar 2026 — an increase of roughly 35%. Fourth-quarter capital expenditure alone reached approximately $41 billion. Those figures are without precedent. $260 billion in a single fiscal year exceeds the annual revenue of all but a handful of companies on the planet, and it is being deployed by one company into data centers, GPUs, CPUs, power and memory. The accounting overlay matters and it has been widely misread. Effective fiscal 2027, Microsoft is extending the estimated useful life of data centers and office buildings from 15 to 25 years. That change affects only the timing of future depreciation, with minimal benefit to fiscal 2027 operating income. The larger effect is on the capex line itself. More future data center leases shift from finance leases, which are included in capital expenditure, to operating leases, which are not. That adjustment brings the calendar 2026 capex expectation to approximately $175 billion while underlying investment plans remain unchanged. Read that carefully: the reported capex number and the actual spending are diverging because of a classification change. Anyone comparing Microsoft's capex line to a peer's without adjusting for lease treatment is comparing different things. The defensive argument management has made against oversupply risk is that capital expenditure is heavily weighted toward short-lived assets — CPUs and GPUs — which carry shorter lead times. Short lead times mean the spending can be throttled quickly if demand disappoints. That flexibility is real and it is the reason a $260 billion program is survivable rather than terminal. The counterargument is that extending data center useful life from 15 to 25 years while simultaneously buying assets described as short-lived is an uncomfortable pairing. Depreciating a building over 25 years is defensible. The GPUs inside it will not last 25 years. The memory shortage is compounding the cost. Soaring memory chip prices stemming from the AI infrastructure buildout are inflating the per-unit cost of every server rack, which means $260 billion buys less capacity than $260 billion would have bought a year ago. Capex is the single biggest swing factor for margins and the stock over the next several quarters. At $493.51 against trailing EPS of $17.95, Microsoft trades at 27.5 times earnings. Market capitalization stands at $3.67 trillion on roughly 7.43 billion shares. That multiple sits below the stock's own history. Microsoft's 10-year average price-to-earnings ratio is 31.52. The 15-year average is 29.46. The 20-year average is 27.43. At 27.5 times, the stock is trading essentially at its two-decade average and 13% below its ten-year average — despite growing revenue 18% and Azure 43%. The comparison to peers frames it further. Meta trades at 24.7 times trailing earnings with a 12-point operating margin collapse and free cash flow down 90.8%. Microsoft trades at 27.5 times with margins intact and a $678 billion contracted backlog. The three-point premium for a materially better business is modest. The analyst distribution is unusually consolidated for a stock this size. The average twelve-month target sits at $572.92, implying 16.1% upside from $493.51. The high estimate is $870. The low estimate is $400, implying 19% downside. Fifty-two analysts recommend buying with zero sell ratings, producing a Strong Buy consensus across 55 covering firms. A zero-sell-rating distribution on a $3.67 trillion company is worth noting as a sentiment reading. It means the entire covering universe agrees on direction and disagrees only on magnitude — the $470 spread between the $400 low and $870 high reflects differing views on how much capex risk is already priced in. The dividend is a rounding error at $0.91 per share most recently declared and a trailing yield of 0.73%, with a payout ratio near 20%. Nobody owns Microsoft for income, but a growing dividend at a 20% payout ratio signals a management team confident enough in cash generation to commit to a rising distribution while spending $260 billion on infrastructure. EBITDA stands at $198.69 billion with an EBITDA margin of 58.39%. A company converting 58 cents of every revenue dollar into operating cash before interest, tax and depreciation has the capacity to fund the capital program internally. The valuation debate reduces to one input: whether fiscal 2027 depreciation on $260 billion of spending compresses the earnings that the 27.5 multiple is applied to. The financial engine underneath the AI story is what makes the capital program possible, and it has held up better than any peer's. Microsoft Cloud revenue exceeded $214 billion for fiscal 2026, up 27%. Total revenue passed $331 billion, up 18%. Fourth-quarter net income reached $35.77 billion on $90.01 billion of revenue — a 39.7% net margin. Third-quarter operating income was $38.4 billion on $82.9 billion of revenue, growing 20% against 18% revenue growth. Operating income growing faster than revenue while capital expenditure runs at $41 billion a quarter is the metric that separates Microsoft from Meta, whose operating margin compressed to 31% from 43%, and from Alphabet, whose free cash flow turned negative at -$5.9 billion. EBITDA at $198.69 billion with a 58.39% margin describes a business with pricing power in enterprise software that no amount of AI competition has yet eroded. Office, Windows, Dynamics and LinkedIn generate the cash that funds Azure's buildout, and Productivity and Business Processes grew 14.3% to $37.85 billion in the fourth quarter — respectable growth from a mature base. The concern flagged by credit analysis earlier this year was cash generation relative to spending. Microsoft has ranked toward the bottom of large software companies on cash generation metrics precisely because the capital program consumes so much of the operating cash flow. That is arithmetic rather than deterioration — the business generates more cash than it ever has, and it spends more than it generates on infrastructure. The company employs 223,000 people. Headcount discipline alongside a $260 billion capital program is the same trade Meta is running: spending on machines while holding the line on people. The balance sheet retains capacity. Microsoft carries one of the small number of remaining top-tier corporate credit ratings, and that access to debt markets at low spreads is a genuine competitive advantage in a capital cycle this large. A competitor without that access has to fund from cash flow or equity. The item to watch in fiscal 2027 is the depreciation line. Extending asset lives from 15 to 25 years pushes charges into later periods, which flatters near-term operating income at the cost of later years. The hyperscaler comparison in the second quarter of calendar 2026 lays out the competitive position precisely. Azure grew 43% in its fourth fiscal quarter and crossed $100 billion in annual revenue. Amazon Web Services grew 37% to $42.23 billion in Amazon's second quarter, with an AI business at a $25 billion annualized run rate. Google Cloud grew 82% to $24.77 billion. By absolute scale, Azure is roughly 2.4 times Amazon's quarterly cloud revenue on an annualized basis and roughly four times Google Cloud. By growth rate, Google Cloud leads, Azure is second and AWS is third. By capital efficiency, Microsoft is the only one of the three that showed a contracted backlog large enough to justify the spending. Alphabet trades at $328.07, down 3.04% today. Its second-quarter revenue reached $119.8 billion, up 24.2%, with the Gemini App at 950 million monthly active users. It spent $44.92 billion on capex in the quarter and suspended its buyback. Google Cloud's 82% growth is genuinely faster than Azure's, and Gemini's consumer reach is larger than anything Microsoft has in consumer AI. Amazon trades at $252.13, down 1.88%. AWS remains the largest infrastructure provider by installed base, and Amazon has the advantage of selling both the compute agents run on and the commerce inventory agents transact against. Microsoft's differentiated position is the enterprise software layer sitting above the cloud. Neither Amazon nor Alphabet owns Office, Windows, Teams, Dynamics, LinkedIn or GitHub. Copilot at 30 million paid seats and GitHub Copilot at 50 million users exist because Microsoft already had the distribution inside the enterprise before AI arrived. That is the same distribution argument Meta is making with WhatsApp, applied to a different market. Microsoft owns the workplace surface. Meta owns the messaging surface. Alphabet owns search and Android. Amazon owns commerce and infrastructure. The nearest competitive threat is that agent capability lets a customer replace the Office layer entirely — an AI that drafts, calculates and presents without needing Word, Excel or PowerPoint underneath it. That is a multi-year risk rather than a quarterly one, and the usage-based billing pivot is Microsoft positioning to monetize the agent even if the application layer erodes. Meta's Muse launch produced a 5.75% move in META, a 3.04% decline in Alphabet, and 44 cents of movement in Microsoft. The reason deserves stating explicitly because it explains what Microsoft actually sells. Muse is a consumer AI agent distributed through WhatsApp and a standalone app, sold on tiered consumer subscriptions to U.S. users aged 18 and over. It books travel, sends emails, fills out forms and makes purchases on an individual's behalf. Copilot is enterprise software. It is sold to IT departments through procurement processes involving security review, compliance certification, data residency requirements and multi-year commitments. Its 30 million paid seats sit inside organizations that have signed contracts contributing to a $678 billion backlog. Those are not competing products. They compete for the same underlying model capability and the same GPU supply, but not for the same buyer, the same budget or the same sales cycle. The market understood that immediately, which is the most encouraging signal in Microsoft's tape today. A market that repriced Alphabet by $135 billion on a consumer agent launch and left Microsoft untouched has correctly identified that Microsoft's revenue is insulated from consumer AI competition. The intersection that does exist is the partnership layer. Meta has collaborations with Microsoft, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom and OpenAI. Meta's Muse Spark models and its $130 billion to $145 billion capital program create demand for the same infrastructure Microsoft is building. Every frontier lab that does not build its own data centers is a potential Azure customer. That is the underappreciated angle. Microsoft's exposure to the consumer agent war is not competitive — it is as a supplier. More consumer agents mean more inference demand, and inference demand runs on cloud infrastructure. Microsoft's own AI products keep shipping alongside the enterprise stack, including the Project Perception cybersecurity system and continued investment across the portfolio. The stock's indifference today is the market saying Microsoft is upstream of the fight. The most persistent overhang on Microsoft is not competitive or financial. It is legal, and it is growing. The Seattle Times Company and Newsday have sued OpenAI and Microsoft in federal court, alleging the companies copied the newspapers' journalism without permission to train AI systems. That follows the closely watched New York Times lawsuit, where recent filings covered a range of copyright law and cultural arguments. Microsoft being sued by the parent company of its hometown daily newspaper is a notable escalation in a litigation trend that now spans multiple publishers across multiple jurisdictions. The financial exposure is difficult to size and that is precisely the problem. Copyright damages in the United States can be assessed per work, and training corpora contain enormous numbers of individual works. A ruling that establishes per-work liability for training data would produce a number that no reserve accounts for. The more consequential risk is structural rather than monetary. An adverse ruling on whether training on copyrighted material constitutes fair use would require licensing arrangements across the industry, which raises the cost of every model Microsoft trains or serves and compresses the margin on AI revenue that the entire investment case depends on. Microsoft's position is complicated by the OpenAI relationship. The company is named alongside OpenAI in these actions, which means it carries litigation exposure for a partner's training decisions as well as its own. Set against that, the practical market treatment has been dismissive. The stock dipped on the latest lawsuit filings and recovered. A $3.67 trillion company with $198.69 billion of EBITDA can absorb settlements measured in billions without a material change to the investment case, and the market is pricing settlements rather than injunctions. That judgment is probably correct and it is not certain. The distinction between a damages award and an injunction on training practices is the difference between a one-time charge and a business model change. For anyone modeling Microsoft over multi-year horizons, the publisher litigation is the tail risk that does not appear in any capex or Azure growth calculation. Upside, in order: $499.70 as Friday's close and the $500 handle, 1.3% above spot. Then the mid-$530s, and $553.72 as the 52-week high, 12.2% above current price. Beyond that, the average twelve-month target at $572.92 implies 16.1% upside, with the high estimate at $870. Downside, in order: $490.15 as Tuesday's low, 0.7% below spot. Then the mid-$460s where the post-earnings gap sits. Then $422.30, the level from which the July repricing began, 14.4% beneath current price. The low analyst estimate sits at $400, implying 19% downside. The 52-week low is $349.20. Base case at 48% probability: Microsoft consolidates between $470 and $520 into the October 27 fiscal first-quarter report. The stock holds its post-earnings gains without extending them, because the next catalyst is a quarter away and the $500 handle needs a reason to break. Target range $480 to $510. Bull case at 33% probability: fiscal Q1 Azure growth comes in at or above the guided 45% constant currency, commercial RPO extends beyond $678 billion, Copilot seat additions maintain their doubling pace, and management holds capex guidance without raising it. The stock clears $500, works through the mid-$530s, and tests $553.72. Upside 12.2%, with $572.92 the twelve-month target. Bear case at 19% probability: Azure growth decelerates below 40%, fiscal 2027 capex guidance moves above $260 billion, or the depreciation line from the useful-life extension proves less flattering than modeled. Add a Federal Reserve hike on September 16 lifting the 10-year through 4.8120%, and a 27.5 multiple compresses toward 24. That takes the stock to roughly $430. Downside 13%. The distribution skews bullish because the $678 billion backlog is contractual rather than aspirational, and because the valuation at 27.5 times sits below the ten-year average of 31.52 and roughly at the twenty-year average of 27.43. The single most important date is October 27. The single most important number is Azure constant-currency growth against the 45% guide. Microsoft at $493.51, down 0.09%, is the least interesting stock on the tape today and the most defensible one. The constructive case is documented and specific. Annual revenue surpassed $331 billion, up 18%. Microsoft Cloud exceeded $214 billion, up 27%. Azure crossed $100 billion in annual revenue growing 43% in the fourth quarter against a guided 39% to 40%, with 45% constant-currency growth guided for the current quarter against a 41.4% consensus. Commercial RPO reached $678 billion, up 84% — more than two years of total company revenue in signed commitments. Copilot passed 30 million paid seats with net additions more than doubling sequentially and GitHub Copilot at 50 million users. Fourth-quarter net income of $35.77 billion on $90.01 billion of revenue is a 39.7% net margin, and EBITDA of $198.69 billion carries a 58.39% margin. The stock trades at 27.5 times trailing earnings against a ten-year average of 31.52, with 52 buy ratings and zero sells. The cautious case is equally real. Fiscal 2027 capital expenditure guidance of $255 billion to $260 billion is a 35% increase on a program that was already the largest in corporate history, and the memory shortage means those dollars buy less capacity than they did a year ago. The useful-life extension from 15 to 25 years and the finance-to-operating lease shift make the reported capex line less comparable to peers and to Microsoft's own history. The stock sits 10.9% below its 52-week high having already run 26.4% in six weeks, which means the good news is in. Publisher litigation alongside OpenAI is expanding rather than resolving. And a 60% probability of a Federal Reserve hike on September 16, with the 10-year at 4.8120%, is the wrong environment for a 27.5 multiple. The verdict is constructive with the catalyst deferred. Microsoft is the only company in the AI capital cycle that has shown the market a contracted demand backlog large enough to justify what it is spending, and $678 billion is the number that separates it from every peer building on conviction alone. Hold $490.15 and the post-earnings structure survives. Clear $500 and the path to $553.72 opens. Between those numbers, ten dollars wide, is a stock waiting for October 27.

title: Agentforce ARR Hits $1.5B: Can It Boost Salesforce's Revenue Growth? - The Globe and Mail
content: Salesforce, Inc.CRM is gaining traction with Agentforce. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027, Agentforce ARR (annual recurring revenue) exceeded $1.5 billion, jumping more than 240% year over year. Combined Agentforce and Data 360 ARR reached nearly $3.9 billion, up more than 210%. These figures show that customers are increasingly willing to pay for AI-powered tools and enterprise data capabilities. Customer usage is also expanding quickly. Salesforce recorded 3.2 billion Agentic Work Units (AWUs) in the second quarter, up 97% sequentially. Bookings for Agentforce One Edition and Agentforce for Apps more than doubled from the previous quarter. This suggests that AI adoption is moving beyond experimentation toward broader use. However, Agentforce is still small compared with Salesforce’s overall business. Second-quarter revenues reached $11.3 billion, up 11% year over year, while subscription and support revenues rose 12% to $10.8 billion. Current remaining performance obligation increased 14% to $33.5 billion, pointing to healthy demand ahead. Buoyed by strong top-line performance, Salesforce raised its fiscal 2027 revenue guidance from $45.90-$46.20 billion to $46.10-$46.40 billion, implying 11%-12% year-over-year growth. It also expects subscription and support revenues to increase slightly above 12%. Agentforce can become a meaningful growth driver, but it will take time to change Salesforce’s growth rate materially. For now, its rapid adoption strengthens the case for steady, rather than explosive, revenue acceleration. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal 2027 revenue is currently pegged at $46.22 billion, indicating an 11.3% year-over-year increase. Microsoft 365 Copilot is already showing strong adoption. Paid seats surpassed 30 million in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, while net seat additions more than doubled sequentially. Customers deploying more than 50,000 seats increased more than sevenfold year over year. Azure and other cloud services revenues also jumped 43%. Oracle is taking a more data-centric approach. Its Oracle AI Database 26ai is designed to serve as a foundation for agentic AI, while AI agents are being embedded across its Fusion Cloud applications. Oracle claims its AI architecture can reduce manual procurement work by 60-80% and lower inventory carrying costs by 15-30%. Its Multicloud AI Database revenues surged 404% year over year in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. Salesforce faces strong competition from Microsoft and Oracle. Microsoft has unmatched scale across cloud and productivity software, while Oracle has deep control over enterprise data and applications. Salesforce does not need to beat its rivals everywhere. Its bigger opportunity is to make Agentforce the leading AI layer for customer relationship management solutions and turn rapid adoption into durable revenue growth. title: Sovereign AI Boost: Palantir Deal Sparks 8% Rise in Nebius Shares - The Globe and Mail
content: Nebius Group N.V.’s NBIS shares jumped 7.73% in trading yesterday and closed the session at $243.88 after Palantir TechnologiesPLTR partnered with Nebius for AI-native cloud infrastructure. The initiative combines Palantir’s enterprise AI software with Nebius’ AI-native cloud and computing infrastructure. It potentially gives Nebius access to a broader pool of enterprises seeking secure, controllable AI infrastructure while reinforcing its position as a major neocloud player. Under the agreement, Nebius will provide AI compute and inference infrastructure to Palantir’s commercial customers. Palantir has designated Nebius as its preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner. Following the integration, NBIS compute and inference endpoints are expected to operate inside PLTR’s enterprise perimeter. Sovereign AI is becoming a priority for governments and businesses seeking greater control over sensitive data, models and computing. Palantir provides the software and control layer, while Nebius supplies the AI infrastructure. The joined forces aim to offer an end-to-end platform that lets customers run open AI models, train them on proprietary data and retain control of their models and workloads. The companies also plan to accelerate capacity deployment through modular data centers at sites with available power. Nebius competes with much larger cloud providers and neoclouds like CoreWeave CRWV and MicrosoftMSFT, making Palantir’s selection as its preferred sovereign AI infrastructure partner a strong endorsement. Furthermore, Palantir could become a key distribution channel, giving its customers access to Nebius infrastructure and helping Nebius reduce customer-acquisition friction and expand into enterprise AI. Nebius reported $582 million of second-quarter revenue, up 454% year over year, and maintained its 2026 revenue outlook of $3-$3.4 billion. The company also expects connected power capacity to reach roughly 800 MW to 1 GW by the end of 2026. This growth is being fueled by the rapid expansion of AI computing demand. In August, CRWV announced that Rescale is expanding its cloud ecosystem to include CoreWeave Cloud. The collaboration gives Rescale customers in aerospace, automotive, energy, life sciences and manufacturing easier access to CRWV’s AI-optimized infrastructure for demanding engineering simulations, HPC and machine learning workloads, potentially accelerating AI adoption across computationally intensive industries. It also won a multi-year agreement with Hudson River Trading to build its next-generation AI-driven research and model-development platform. The deployment will use NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72 platform and Spectrum-X Ethernet networking. CRWV is strengthening its AI infrastructure strategy through a multi-year agreement with Solidigm that provides priority access to enterprise SSD capacity. Its AI investments are converting into measurable commercial traction across its stack. Multi-model flexibility, paired with continued access to OpenAI's frontier models under an IP arrangement extending to 2032, allows customers to optimize cost and performance while keeping Microsoft central to their AI infrastructure decisions. With demand still outpacing available capacity, this positioning across AI infrastructure, tooling and applications should continue widening Microsoft's addressable opportunity heading into fiscal 2027. However, Microsoft’s AI and cloud buildout is consuming a larger share of company resources. Microsoft (MSFT) just made a major change that could give investors a much clearer view of where its growth is coming from, particularly as artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes its business. Earlier this month, the company announced plans to overhaul how it reports its business segments ahead of its first-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings results in October. Microsoft previously reported revenue across three segments: Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. Starting with Q1 2027, however, these three segments will be condensed into just two: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. Agents and Infra will include Microsoft 365, GitHub, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions, frontier and support services, and Azure. Meanwhile, Devices and Consumer will include search, advertising, Xbox, and Windows OEM and devices. But the bigger takeaway for investors is what Microsoft plans to disclose within the segments. Dear Nvidia Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for September 10 Rocket Lab Keeps Landing Defense Deals. Here's Why Analysts Aren't Getting More Bullish. Why Stifel Just Revamped Its Price Target for Microsoft Stock Markets move fast. Keep up by reading our FREE midday Barchart Brief newsletter for exclusive charts, analysis, and headlines. For the first time, the company will report quarterly revenue for its Azure cloud business, giving investors a much clearer picture of the performance of its cloud operation as it competes directly with Amazon's (AMZN) Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Alphabet's (GOOGL) Google Cloud. In addition to Azure, Microsoft will also provide greater transparency into quarterly revenue across key businesses, including M365 Cloud, Industry Solutions, and Ads. The move comes as AI increasingly cuts across Microsoft's products and services, changing what the company builds, how it operates, and how its various businesses fit together. For investors, the new reporting structure could make Microsoft's financial picture easier to decipher. Rather than relying on broader segment numbers, Wall Street will have more visibility into the performance of individual businesses, with Azure's revenue disclosure potentially being the most important addition. So, with Microsoft gearing up to give investors a sharper view of its business health and AI-driven growth, here's a closer look at MSFT stock. Founded in 1975, Microsoft has grown from a modest software company into a global technology leader. Headquartered in Redmond, Washington, the company has played a major role in shaping modern computing through widely used products such as Windows, Office, Teams, and Xbox, which have become an integral part of how people work, connect, and entertain themselves. Over the years, Microsoft has expanded its focus by investing heavily in cloud computing through Azure, helping businesses operate more digitally and efficiently. Now, the company is accelerating its push into AI, embedding AI-powered tools across its platforms to boost productivity and reshape how users interact with technology. That said, while Microsoft's leadership and rapid innovation in cloud and AI remain undeniable, MSFT stock hasn't been getting the same love from investors lately. Shares have been largely weighed down by surging capital expenditures related to AI infrastructure. Despite being one of the most valuable companies in the world with a massive market capitalization of roughly $3.7 trillion, MSFT stock is up only marginally year-to-date (YTD) and down by less than 1% for the past 52 weeks. That performance trails the broader S&P 500 Index ($SPX), which has climbed about 18% over the past year and 12% so far in 2026. However, the picture looks considerably brighter in the near term. Microsoft's latest earnings report showed solid growth in Azure, helping reignite investor enthusiasm and push the stock 20% higher over the past three months, easily beating the broader market's 4% gain over the same period. Microsoft delivered a strong Q4 performance on July 29, comfortably clearing Wall Street expectations as sustained momentum in commercial cloud infrastructure and expanding AI workloads powered growth. Revenue reached $90 billion, up 18% year-over-year (YOY) and ahead of Wall Street's forecast of $87.4 billion. Adjusted EPS came in at $4.74, up 23% YOY and well above the $4.21 consensus estimate. Operating income also climbed 18% to $40.6 billion. The cloud story remained the biggest catalyst. Microsoft Cloud revenue surged 27% YOY to $59.3 billion, while commercial remaining performance obligations (RPO) jumped 84% to $678 billion, highlighting the strength of future contracted revenue. The standout performer was the Intelligent Cloud segment, where quarterly revenue climbed 32% to $39.3 billion. Azure and related cloud services accelerated with 43% YOY growth, fueled by broad enterprise adoption of computing capacity and custom AI deployments. Microsoft's Productivity and Business Processes segment also continued to expand, with revenue rising 14% YOY to $37.8 billion. Within the segment, Microsoft 365 Consumer cloud revenue increased 24%, LinkedIn revenue rose 12%, and Dynamics 365 revenue climbed 13%. In contrast, the More Personal Computing division remained the company's primary operational drag, with revenue declining 4% YOY to $12.9 billion. Persistent weakness in hardware demand weighed on Windows OEM and Devices revenue, which fell 7%, while Xbox content and services declined 10%. Microsoft's AI ambitions were also reflected in the scale of its ecosystem. During full-year 2026, management highlighted that Azure revenue surpassed $100 billion for the first time, while Microsoft 365 Copilot surpassed 30 million paid seats, underscoring growing customer adoption of Microsoft's AI offerings and its role in helping businesses pursue AI transformation. At the same time, Microsoft continued returning capital to investors, distributing $10.2 billion through dividends and share repurchases during Q4. However, capital expenditures emerged as the key concern for investors. Total quarterly capex and finance lease additions surged to $41 billion, as Microsoft continued investing heavily in data-center construction and GPU clusters to support its growing AI infrastructure needs. Looking ahead to Q1 2027, Microsoft expects revenue to land between $89.85 billion and $90.95 billion, representing growth of 16% to 17%. The company also expects capex spending to exceed $50 billion for the upcoming quarter. Wall Street remains firmly bullish on Microsoft, with MSFT stock carrying a consensus "Strong Buy" rating. Of the 51 analysts covering MSFT stock, 41 recommend a "Strong Buy," six have a "Moderate Buy" rating, and just four have a "Hold" rating, leaving little doubt about the Street's confidence in the tech giant. The bull case also comes with meaningful upside potential. The average price target of $559.76 points to roughly 13% potential upside from current levels, while the Street-high target of $700 suggests Microsoft could rally as much as 42% from current levels. title: Amazon CEO Andy Jassy Explained Why Semiconductor Sales Could Keep Climbing for Years to Come. Here's My Favorite AI Chipmaker Right Now. - The Globe and Mail
content: Even if hyperscalers' spending growth slows, semiconductor sales could rise at a fast pace. Nvidia and Broadcom have seen sales explode as they provide key chips for the largest AI data centers. This company is even better positioned to provide sustainable earnings growth well into the future. Semiconductor companies have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the massive AI data center build-out over the last few years. Companies like Nvidia(NASDAQ: NVDA) and Broadcom(NASDAQ: AVGO) are at the center of the industry, with their leading AI accelerator chips. Other chipmakers specializing in memory or networking chips have also seen profits soar and their stock prices rise. And the incredible growth could continue for years to come. PwC expects total capital expenditures for data centers to climb from $800 billion this year to $1.8 trillion by 2050. More importantly, it's how that spending will be allocated that makes that estimate so bullish for semiconductor stocks. Amazon(NASDAQ: AMZN) CEO Andy Jassy explained on the company's most recent earnings call that spending will shift toward more semiconductors, suggesting there's a lot of room for revenue growth in semiconductor stocks. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » But Nvidia and Broadcom might not be the best semiconductor stocks right now. Another industry giant could be an even better opportunity to play the long-term growth potential in chips. When you dig under the hood of hyperscalers' massive capital expenditure budgets, there are two core components: the data center buildings and the servers and networking equipment inside them. As Jassy points out, "these have different capital cycles." Data centers depreciate much more slowly than the server racks full of GPUs. "For our data centers, which have 30-plus-year useful lives, we should get at least five to six generations of server economics," Jassy told analysts during Amazon's second-quarter earnings call. "This means in the short term, when demand is necessitating so many data centers being built simultaneously in advance of when we can start monetizing them, we'll spend a lot of capex and encounter free cash flow headwinds until these data centers come online, can be monetized, and we get a few years into these servers being utilized." In other words, once a data center is built, Amazon doesn't have to build the data center again. However, it does have to periodically refresh the chips inside of it. As a result, over time, more and more of its capital expenditures will go toward semiconductors. The same is true at all the other hyperscalers. In fact, Microsoft(NASDAQ: MSFT) CFO Amy Hood said she's already seeing the shift happen for the company's competing Azure cloud computing business. "You've seen our capex really pivot toward what I would call and do call short-lived assets," she said on Microsoft's fourth-quarter earnings call. She noted roughly two-thirds of Microsoft's capex currently goes toward GPUs, CPUs, and other equipment for data centers. PwC's estimates suggest a significant slowdown in spending at some point over the next decade. But if chips make up a significantly larger portion of the budget in the future, the growth in semiconductor spending can climb at a relatively high pace. That bodes well for one semiconductor stock in particular. Nvidia's leading GPU systems are very likely to retain a significant portion of AI spending well into the future. It's establishing partnerships and even providing funding to ensure its chips continue to find their way into big data centers. That said, there's a growing push toward custom silicon among the hyperscalers. Jassy noted that it's bringing more of its own Trainium chips into its data centers than Nvidia chips this year during Amazon's first-quarter earnings call. Meanwhile, Broadcom is experiencing tremendous growth for its AI business, which includes its partnership co-developing and engineering Alphabet's (NASDAQ: GOOG)(NASDAQ: GOOGL) popular TPU chips. The company recently reported quarterly AI-related revenue growth of 221% with expectations for that number to accelerate next quarter. But the semiconductor company best positioned to benefit over the long run is Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing(NYSE: TSM). The largest contract chip manufacturer in the world works with Nvidia, Broadcom, and almost every other fabless chip designer in the world. It benefits from both its scale and its leading technology, creating a virtuous cycle that's only strengthening amid the AI build-out. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, or TSMC as it's known, has grown its market share of third-party chip manufacturing to 73%. That provides huge amounts of revenue ($143 billion over the past 12 months) with which it can reinvest in research and development and additional manufacturing capacity. That allows it to maintain its leading technological capabilities in designing the world's most advanced chips for AI data centers while supplying the capacity hyperscalers demand. That, in turn, ensures it wins more contracts with Nvidia, Broadcom, and everyone else in the future. No matter which chips hyperscalers decide to put in their data centers, it's very likely they'll be manufactured by TSMC. The stock trades for less than 25 times earnings, despite expectations for revenue growth of around 25% per year and potential for even better earnings growth. title: How Microsoft AI is helping Cognizant scale Delivery Excellence across 10,000 projects - Microsoft Source
content: Microsoft AI is changing what sits between a Cognizant delivery leader and the decision they need to make. With more than 350,000 associates, over 10,000 projects and 2,000-plus customers, scale has long been both Cognizant’s strength and its pressure point. Few functions feel that scale more acutely than Delivery Excellence (DEx), whose leaders are responsible for quality, governance and consistent execution across thousands of customer engagements. Using Microsoft AI Foundry, Azure AI services and Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cognizant is reimagining how those leaders work. A few years ago, much of a DEx leader’s day disappeared into finding the right version of a process document, pulling service-level data out of an incident system or re-reading a statement of work before a client call. “That work is not intellectually demanding, but it interrupts deeper thinking and client focus,” says Pandiyan Adiyapatham, Assistant Vice President, Business CIO, Delivery Excellence at Cognizant. Pandiyan and his team saw an opportunity to redesign how DEx work gets done, moving leaders from finding information to acting on it. “What changed was the work between the systems and the delivery leader,” he says. Cognizant’s core systems remain in place, but AI now handles reading documents, reconciling data, surfacing risks and preparing drafts for the team to review. The agent ecosystem powers retrieval, reasoning and workflow orchestration while embedding these experiences directly into familiar tools such as Teams, Outlook, Word and Excel. Behind the scenes, a network of agents connects delivery, audit and knowledge workflows. The ‘delivery layer’ monitors live projects that track contract obligations, predict risks and analyze client sentiment. The ‘audit layer’ supports assurance, reviewing commitments and drafting corrective actions before assessments begin. The ‘knowledge and innovation’ layer turns institutional memory into a reusable asset, surfacing relevant project context and insights in real time. “It would be humanly impossible to track all these signals — delivery, risk and customer sentiment — simultaneously. That’s where AI becomes powerful,” explains Pandiyan. Guardrails are built into every workflow: zero-trust access, fine-grained permissions, and full auditability within a controlled Azure environment, with continuous feedback loops improving output quality. The platform saw rapid adoption, growing from 6,700 users in its early rollout to more than 8,000 users as of June 2026. “People found it useful and brought others in,” Pandiyan says. “Agents became infrastructure quietly, which signals genuine utility rather than compliance.” The biggest surprise wasn’t accuracy, but ownership. “The anticipated worry had been whether the agent would get it right, but the real friction turned out to be ownership. The question became who is accountable when the agent drafts and the assessor approves.” The debate reinforced human accountability for final decisions. The knowledge maturity assessment agent, for instance, has a 42 percent recommendation acceptance rate. “That is not a failure metric,” Pandiyan says. “It’s the governance model working as intended.” For Cognizant, the outcome is a fundamental shift in how leaders spend their time, focusing more on customers, risk management and business decisions. “Reviewing every statement of work took time and sometimes a commitment could slip through. Now the agent securely extracts and tracks SOW obligations and presents them in a format that makes them easier to review and assess. I still make the final decision, but I can do it faster and with greater confidence.” L. Vedavalli, Director-Delivery Excellence, Cognizant

title: Constellation Energy's Biggest AI Power Deal Doesn't Start Paying Until June 2027 - The Globe and Mail
content: Meta agreed to buy the clean energy attributes of the Clinton plant's 1,121 megawatts of nuclear output for 20 years, starting in June 2027. The plant is supported today by an Illinois zero-emission credit program, which the Meta agreement replaces when it expires in mid-2027. Constellation raised its 2026 adjusted operating earnings guidance to $11.50 to $12.50 per share, with a midpoint about 28% above last year's result. In June of last year, Meta Platforms(NASDAQ:META) agreed to buy the clean energy attributes of Constellation Energy's (NASDAQ:CEG) Clinton Clean Energy Center in Illinois for 20 years. The agreement covers 1,121 megawatts of nuclear generation -- more output than Constellation has committed to any other artificial intelligence (AI) buyer. The next-biggest is the roughly 835-megawatt agreement that is restarting a Three Mile Island unit for Microsoft. But the Meta contract doesn't commence until June 2027, nine months from now. And it means the results Constellation is reporting today, including the guidance it raised with last month's second-quarter report, don't include a dollar from the company's biggest AI agreement. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » For investors who own the stock as a way to play AI's power demand, I think the calendar is worth getting straight. Shares go for about $299 as of this writing. Their high over the past year was $412.70. The growth the market is paying for arrives on a schedule. The social media company is purchasing Clinton's clean energy attributes for two decades as part of its commitment to match 100% of its electricity use with clean and renewable energy. The plant's power itself keeps flowing onto the local grid. The agreement also supported relicensing the facility, and regulators granted the renewal in December 2025, clearing Clinton to run through 2047. And plant upgrades will add 30 megawatts of output along the way. The June 2027 start date isn't arbitrary. Clinton is supported today by Illinois's ratepayer-funded zero-emission credit program, and the Meta agreement begins when that program expires. In other words, the plant is being paid right now. The deal changes who pays for Clinton's clean energy attributes, not whether anyone does. The Meta contract is one item in a queue. Constellation's 20-year agreement with Microsoft begins when the Crane Clean Energy Center, the former Three Mile Island unit, comes back online. Regulators have approved transferring interconnection rights to the site from two Pennsylvania fossil-fuel units Constellation had planned to retire, along with a fuel license amendment -- progress the company said moves the plant closer to restarting in 2027. Constellation's second-quarter update also disclosed 920 megawatts of new long-term contracts to sell nuclear power, signed with investment-grade customers on 15-to-20-year terms with start dates from 2029 through 2032. Among them is a 176-megawatt deal with Walmart that will support a 30-megawatt capacity expansion at Constellation's Dresden plant in Illinois. So the contracted demand arrives in stages -- Meta in June 2027, the Crane restart the same year, and the newest agreements from 2029 on. Not one of them adds anything to this year's results. The queue matters because Constellation's earnings are climbing without it. Constellation's non-GAAP (adjusted) operating earnings rose to $2.55 per share in the second quarter of 2026, about 34% higher than the $1.91 it earned a year earlier. The company credited the addition of Calpine, the natural gas and geothermal generator it acquired in January, along with favorable market and portfolio conditions, partially offset by nuclear outages. Constellation also lifted its guidance for the full year and now expects adjusted operating earnings of $11.50 to $12.50 per share in 2026. Showing how much growth is arriving before any AI contract kicks in, the midpoint of that range sits about 28% above the $9.39 per share the company earned last year. In short, the earnings the stock is priced against are moving higher on their own, with the contracted nuclear deals stacked on top starting in the middle of next year. Shares trade at about 25 times earnings, measured against the midpoint of Constellation's 2026 guidance. It's a premium price for a power producer, but I'd argue it's attached to unusually visible growth: the customers are signed and the start dates are on paper. Of course, contracted isn't the same as guaranteed. The plants have to run, the Crane restart could slip, and a 20-year agreement can't pull its start date forward. But growth backed by signed contracts is arguably easier to count on than growth that depends on demand that may never show up. Constellation's biggest AI deal starts paying next June. Until then, the earnings carrying the stock don't need it. title: Microsoft's OpenAI Partnership Draws Fresh Legal Fire - TradingView
content: Microsoft MSFT shares fell more than 1.5% Tuesday as two additional news organizations deepened the legal fight over AI training data. The Seattle Times and Newsday are suing Microsoft and OpenAI, alleging their paywalled journalism was used to train AI models. The claims add to litigation involving The New York Times (NYT) and Ziff Davis, turning isolated copyright disputes into a broader risk for Microsoft's AI strategy. The unusual wrinkle is that The Seattle Times and Newsday previously joined an AI partnership initiative. Both received funding from the $10 million AI Collaborative and Fellowship Grant to hire AI fellows. That relationship makes questions about permission, licensing, and the boundaries of collaboration important. For investors, the financial impact remains uncertain. Microsoft is large enough to absorb legal expenses, and its cloud and software businesses are not dependent on one publisher group. The risk is precedent. If courts determine that paywalled articles require compensation or explicit licensing before being used for model training, AI development could become more expensive. Settlements could also encourage additional publishers to pursue claims, while restrictions on training data could complicate how OpenAI improves future models. The stock's modest gain of 0.26% over the past year suggests investors are already demanding clearer returns from Microsoft's enormous AI spending. Fresh legal uncertainty adds another issue to that debate, even if Tuesday's decline cannot be attributed entirely to the lawsuits. Microsoft also faces a separate consumer concern around Grand Theft Auto VI. Questions remain about how the highly anticipated game will perform on the less powerful Xbox Series S, with reports warning of possible performance drawbacks in intense situations. That gaming issue is smaller than the AI dispute, but both highlight the same investor concern: Microsoft must convert major technology bets into growth while controlling legal, technical, and reputational risks.
